open-question.question: Which tracked paths does the milestones tool count as this project's live milestones: every match of `**/milestones/*/requirements.md` over `git ls-files`, which in this repository also matches the agy test fixture's `tests/fixtures/agy_project/milestones/milestone_01_pocket-ledger-foundations/` and so would list it under `live`, let it hold the root scope against every milestone here the first time its task list is edited, and join its `TASKS_TODO.md` in the `tasks` query once that query's root anchor is swapped for the same pattern, or a narrower rule that leaves a nested project's matches out?

Are the tree-side queries (`live`, `gate`) and the history-side queries (`tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) subcommands of the one `milestones.py`, or two tools, given that every tool under `core/tools/` is one self-contained file copied byte-identical into each host, and that the tree-side half reads `git ls-files` and one path-scoped log per live milestone while the history-side half reads commit subjects and bodies?
open-question.alternative: All six queries (`live`, `gate`, `tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) are subcommands of the one `core/tools/milestones.py`. It keeps its name, its one parser, its one `Error:` contract and help text, and its one git runner with the fixed `GIT_SETTINGS`. The discovery pattern is defined once in it and read by `live` and `gate`, by the live branches of `milestones` and `summary`, and by the `tasks` join once its root anchor is swapped for that pattern. No file is added under `core/tools/`. Its tests stay in the existing `test_milestones_*` files on the conftest git fixtures, and the five `tasks` call sites stay unchanged. Any later split is left to whichever later milestone finds a reason for one. The query set does not actually divide cleanly at the tree/history line. `milestones` and `summary` both list or describe live milestones by scope, and the `tasks` join will move onto the discovery pattern. Keeping everything in one self-contained file means the pattern, the git runner, and the error contract each have one home, rather than copies that must stay identical between two files the parity rule forbids from importing each other. It also matches the draft, which names the tool `core/tools/milestones.py` and has its tree-side half "gained" by that tool. The file grows from 353 lines and one query to six queries now, with `since` and `show` still to come in step 4. That makes it the second-largest tool after `open_questions.py`. It also mixes two git read shapes (an `ls-files` listing with one path-scoped log per milestone, and whole-log subject and body parsing) and possibly two output contracts behind one `--help`. How different `gate`'s exit contract becomes depends on the sibling question that owns the gate's output.

The tool is split into two self-contained, stdlib-only files at the line the question draws, each copied byte-identical into every host and importing no sibling. `core/tools/milestones.py` keeps the history-side queries (`tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`), so its name, its five `tasks` call sites, and its five test files stay as they are. A new tool file holds the tree-side queries (`live`, `gate`), with its own parser, help text, `Error:` contract, parity test, and test files. Each file carries its own copy of the git runner, the error type and main, and the discovery pattern: the history side needs that pattern for its live branches of `milestones` and `summary` and for the swapped `tasks` join. Each file reads git one way and has one job. The tree-side tool is what the resolution stop and the four gate sites call before any write, and it would be small, testable on its own fixtures, and readable in one sitting. The history tool stays a pure reader of commit subjects and bodies, so later history queries (`since`, `show`) grow that file without touching the one the gate depends on. The split follows the tools' existing convention of one file per concern (each document writer and the commit tool are separate files). The discovery pattern, the git settings, and the error contract are written twice, and the self-contained rule leaves nothing but a test to keep the two copies agreeing. A change to the pattern, such as the narrower rule a sibling question may set, has to be made in both files, and a missed copy makes `live` and `milestones` disagree about which milestones exist. It also adds a seventh tool file, a new name for runners and docs, and CLAUDE.md layout and invariant text describing two tools where the draft describes one.

The split is made at the check-versus-listing line instead of the tree-versus-history line. `core/tools/milestones.py` keeps every listing query (`live`, `tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) under one uniform "print lines, exit 0, print nothing for an empty result" contract. A new self-contained tool file holds only `gate`, the one query the four writer sites chain ahead of their write. It carries its own copy of the discovery pattern, the git runner, and the error contract, imports no sibling, and is copied byte-identical into every host with its own parity and contract tests. The one query whose exit status carries meaning (a held scope stops a chained write) lives apart from the readers, whose contract stays exactly as `tasks` states it today. `milestones.py` therefore needs no second exit-status rule in its help text. The gate tool is small enough that its blocking behaviour can be pinned on its own, and the discovery pattern is duplicated once rather than spread across two halves that both list milestones. It still duplicates the discovery pattern and the git runner between two files, with only a test to keep them in agreement. The benefit also depends on the gate's output contract really differing from the readers', which the sibling question on the gate's output owns: if the gate ends up printing and exiting like every other query, the split separates a query that is no different. It also adds a tool file and a name to the layout and docs for a single subcommand.

This option rejects the premise that every tool is one self-contained file. The tree-side queries (`live`, `gate`) and the history-side queries (`tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) become two tool files, with `milestones.py` keeping the history side and its five call sites. Both import one new stdlib-only helper module under `core/tools/` holding the discovery pattern, the git runner with its fixed settings, and the error type and main. The module is copied into every host beside them. The parity tests and the self-contained invariant in CLAUDE.md are revised to allow this one shared module, which CLAUDE.md already notes a later milestone may extract. The two halves each get their own file, help text, and tests, and the discovery pattern and git runner still have exactly one home. A change to the pattern, or the shallow-clone handling a sibling question may add to both halves, is made once, and the two tools cannot drift apart on which milestones exist. It breaks a rule every tool keeps today: one runnable file, importing no sibling, asserted by parity tests in each tool's suite. A tool becomes runnable only beside its module, so a copy, a rename, or a host layout that separates them fails at import. It also widens the milestone with an invariant change, a parity-test rewrite, and a decision about whether the other tools should then share the module too, in a milestone already sized at about fourteen tasks.

open-question.question: Which fields does one line of the `live` query carry, in what order and with what separator, and how is a started milestone told from a merely defined one on its line, given that the draft lists path, whether it is started, and title, that `tasks` prints tab-separated fields with the title last, and that the resolution stop prints these lines beneath its fixed line for a retry to copy a path from?
open-question.alternative: Three tab-separated fields, as the draft lists them: the milestone path in its canonical printed form first, then a state field holding one of two fixed words, `started` or `defined`, then the title, read from the `requirements.md` heading, last. `live` runs the started test (one path-scoped `git log -1 --diff-filter=M` per live milestone) to fill the state field. It follows the draft and the `tasks` precedent (tab separator, title last, so a spaced title stays unambiguous), puts the path at the start of the line where a retry under the resolution stop copies it, and states the started fact as a plain word that a person and a parser read the same way, which the starting state's in-flight read can use directly. `live` stops reading the tree alone, as the draft's tool paragraph says it does, and pays one log call per live milestone even for the resolution stop, which needs only paths. It adds a two-word vocabulary that the help text and the docs must pin. The title field depends on the heading form, an axis the heading-and-title sibling owns.

Three tab-separated fields with the state word first: `started` or `defined`, then the path, then the title last. The column order matches the draft's `milestones` line (state, finish date, path, title) minus the date. `live` runs the started test per live milestone, as in Path state title. A `live` line reads as a `milestones` line without its date column, so the two milestone listings share one field order and one parser, and started milestones are easy to pick out when scanning the column. The path a retry copies is no longer at the start of the line, so a person has to skip a word to copy it from the resolution stop. Whether the shared order holds depends on the shape the milestones-query-line sibling settles. It carries the same per-milestone log cost and heading dependence as Path state title.

Three tab-separated fields: the path first, then the started test's own print as the state field (the abbreviated hash of the newest commit that modified the milestone's `TASKS_TODO.md` when it is started, and the fixed placeholder `-` when it is merely defined, the same placeholder `tasks` prints for a missing join), then the title last. The field is the gate's own evidence, printed unchanged, with no new vocabulary. A reader can `git show` the hash to see which task entry or completion started the milestone, and the `-` placeholder reuses a convention the tool already has. The hash changes with every completion, so it means "started" only by not being `-`. A person reading the resolution stop must know that convention to tell the two states apart. It keeps the per-milestone log cost and the heading dependence.

Two tab-separated fields: the path, then the state word, `started` or `defined`. No title is printed, so the slug in the path is the only name a line carries. `live` runs the started test per live milestone. `live` never parses `requirements.md`, so its print is independent of whatever heading form the definition tool ends up writing. The slug already comes from the title, so a line still names its milestone in words. It departs from the draft's field list. A five-word slug is a truncated, lowercased title, so the resolution stop and the in-flight read show less than the milestone's own name. A title wanted later means changing the line shape every caller parses.

Two tab-separated fields: the path, then the title last, with no started field. `live` reads the tree alone (`git ls-files` and each `requirements.md` heading). Started is the gate's to compute and print, and a started milestone is not told from a defined one on a `live` line at all. It keeps the draft's own sentence that `live` reads the tree alone and `gate` adds the log. The resolution stop, `live`'s one caller in this milestone that prints its lines, needs no state and pays no log call per milestone. A shallow clone cannot make the line wrong. It rejects the draft's premise that a line says whether its milestone is started. The starting state's in-flight read, which the draft has report each overlapping milestone by path and started state, would need the state from another query or a second shape later, a change for the next milestone. It depends on the heading form the heading-and-title sibling owns.

One field: the path of each live milestone, one per line, with no state, no title, and no separator. This is the shape today's resolution stop prints (one directory name per line) and the shape the draft gives `gate`'s holders. `live` reads the tree alone. It is the simplest contract. It matches the stop's listing as it stands and the gate's holder lines, so every milestone listing in this milestone is a bare path, and nothing in it can drift with the heading form or the started test. It drops both of the draft's other fields. A person retrying has only the slug to choose by, the in-flight read gets neither the state nor the title, and adding either later changes the shape every caller parses.

The draft's three fields in its order (path, then `started` or `defined`, then title last), separated by runs of spaces padded so the columns line up across the whole print instead of by a tab. `live` runs the started test per live milestone. The resolution stop is read by a person choosing a path to retry with, and aligned columns are the easiest form for a person to scan. It breaks the convention that the tab is every tool's listing separator. A path holding a space can no longer be split from the state field reliably, and the padding requires measuring the whole list before printing the first line. A runner parsing the line needs a rule unlike the one it uses for `tasks`.

open-question.question: Does the `live` query take its optional PATH filter (listing only the live milestones whose scope contains PATH or lies under it) in this milestone, or land as the unfiltered list alone, given that its callers here, the resolution stop and the gate, need no filter, that the next milestone's starting-state refresh is the first caller that does, and that a query lands with its first caller?

The `live` query lands in this milestone with its optional PATH filter as the draft's first cut gives it: it lists only the live milestones whose scope contains PATH or lies under it. No runner in this milestone passes PATH: the resolution stop and the gate call the query unfiltered. The filter's first runtime caller is the next milestone's starting-state refresh. The `live` query lands in this milestone with its optional PATH filter (scope contains PATH or lies under it). The premise that no caller here needs the filter is rejected by giving the filter a caller in this milestone: `discuss-milestone-goal`, when it proposes a placement, runs `live` on the proposed scope. The placement proposal, a duty this milestone already gives `discuss-milestone-goal`, gains the one fact that decides whether the proposed scope is free or held. A user is warned before defining a milestone that cannot start until a holder finishes. open-question.question: What does the `gate` query print and exit with when another started milestone overlaps the named milestone's scope, given that the draft proposes the holders one path per line on stdout with exit 1, that every sibling tool's non-zero exit is one `Error:` line on stderr, that a runner chains the gate ahead of its write behind `&&`, and that a held scope is a wait rather than a failure?
open-question.alternative: The draft as written. A held scope prints the holders on stdout, one bare milestone path per line in the canonical printed form, and exits 1; a clear scope prints nothing and exits 0; every failure stays one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1 and nothing on stdout. Held and failed share the exit status and are told apart by which stream printed. The tool's output and error contract gains one stated exception for `gate`. A runner chains `gate && <write>` with no shell test of its own, so the write never runs on a held scope, and each holder line is exactly the string a later `--milestone` or finish call takes, ready to copy from beneath the stop line. It breaks the contract every sibling tool keeps, under which exit 1 always means one `Error:` line on stderr and nothing on stdout: a runner or harness reading the exit status alone cannot tell a wait from a broken git, and every call site has to inspect the streams to pick between its held stop line and its failed-check stop line.

Exit semantics as the draft's (held exits 1 with the holders on stdout, clear exits 0 printing nothing, failures one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1), but each holder is printed as its own `live` query line verbatim rather than as a bare path, so the stop shows the holder's title beside its path in the same field order and separator `live` uses. The person reading the stop sees which milestone holds the scope by its title as well as its path, and the tool has one holder-line shape across `live` and `gate`, with no second format to test or document. It carries the same shared-exit-1 break of the sibling contract as the draft, and it ties the gate's print to the `live` line's fields, so whatever the Live line fields question settles (the started marker, which is redundant on a holder that is by definition started, included) is printed here too; a copy of the path means cutting one field out of a tab-separated line.

alternative.id: Paths on stdout, own exit code

open-question.alternative: A held scope prints the holders on stdout, one bare path per line, and exits with a dedicated status reserved for "held" (for instance 3, clear of argparse's 2 and git's 128); a clear scope prints nothing and exits 0; every failure stays one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1, exactly as every sibling tool's. The contract states the new status as the gate's one addition. Exit 1 keeps its plugin-wide meaning of a failure with an `Error:` line, the `&&` chain still stops the write on a held scope, and the call can tell a wait from a failure by status alone, so a fixed call or a harness branches on the code and never reads a stream or an error's wording. It introduces the first exit status other than 0, 1, and 2 in any tool under `core/tools/`, and every gated call has to capture and branch on that status inside its one shell call to print the right stop line, which is extra fixed shell text at each of the four sites.

A dedicated held status (for instance 3) as in the previous option, clear exiting 0 with nothing printed and failures one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1, but each holder printed as its `live` query line verbatim rather than a bare path. It keeps exit 1's sibling-wide meaning and status-only branching while giving the operator the holder's title in the stop, in the one line shape the `live` query already prints. It pays both costs at once: a new exit status branched on at every site, and a print bound to whatever the Live line fields question settles for `live`, with a started field that is always the same on a holder and a path that has to be cut out of the line to be copied.

`gate` is an ordinary query under the unchanged contract: it prints the holders on stdout, one bare path per line, and exits 0 whether or not the scope is held, printing nothing when it is clear; only a failure exits 1, with one `Error:` line on stderr. The gate holds only through the runner's test for empty output, made either inside the one shell call (the print captured and tested empty ahead of the write behind `&&`) or as a separate check step before the write, as `derive-tasks` step 2 already tests `list` for empty. It needs no exception to the shared output contract and reads a held scope as what it is, a no-failure result like the commit tool's exit-0 no-op, while keeping bare paths ready to copy; the tool stays a pure query that any reader, the next milestone's starting-state refresh included, can call without its print being treated as an error. A bare `gate && <write>` chain proceeds straight through a held scope, so the gate's force rests on every site carrying the emptiness test exactly; a site that drops it, or a runner that rewrites the call, silently defeats the sequencing the pointer used to hold, and each chained form adds a captured value to the call.

`gate` is an ordinary query exiting 0 whether held or clear, as in the previous option, with only a failure exiting 1 on one `Error:` line, the runner testing the print for empty; each holder is printed as its `live` query line verbatim rather than a bare path. No contract exception and no new status, and the stop shows each holder's title in the one line shape `live` prints, so `gate` reads as `live` narrowed to the overlapping started milestones. It keeps the exit-0 option's risk that a call missing the emptiness test runs its write through a held scope, and adds the dependence on the Live line fields question's outcome, with a redundant started field and a path to cut out of each line.

A held scope is reported as a refusal under the unchanged contract: one `Error:` line on stderr naming every holder's path within that one line, nothing on stdout, exit 1; a clear scope prints nothing and exits 0; every other failure is likewise one `Error:` line with exit 1. Each runner stops on one fixed line for a refused gate whatever the cause, with the tool's `Error:` line verbatim beneath it. Nothing in the tool family's contract changes and each site has exactly one gate condition and one stop line, the `&&` chain stopping the write on either cause, in line with the convention that a refused tool call is one condition whose `Error:` line tells the reasons apart. It rejects the premise that a held scope is a wait rather than a failure: the fixed line no longer tells a harness whether to wait for a holder's finish or to repair the environment, which only the error's wording now says and which no runner may classify, and the holders arrive folded into one line instead of one path per line to copy.

What does the `summary` query print for a live milestone, and how does its print tell a live milestone from a finished one, given that for a finished milestone it prints the finish commit's body (title line, blank line, bullets) with its date, and that the draft says a live one prints its goal and the fact that it is live?
open-question.alternative: One three-part shape for both states. The first line is a single field: the finish commit's author date for a finished milestone, the fixed word `live` for a live one. The finished body (title line, blank line, bullets) or, for a live milestone, the title from the `requirements.md` heading, a blank line, and the whole `## Goal` section body follows verbatim, with its outer blank lines trimmed, read from the working tree. Live is told from finished by the first line alone. No date is printed for a live milestone, and live and defined are not told apart. One parser reads both prints, because they share the same three parts and the first line alone tells the state. The live print needs no log read beyond what the tool already does, and it invents no date for a milestone that has not finished. The first line holds a date in one state and a word in the other, so a reader cannot treat it as one typed field. The goal is printed whole, and that can be long: this milestone's goal is one paragraph of about 1,500 characters. Whether `live` matches the state word on the `milestones` line depends on the Milestones query line question.

The first line is two tab-separated fields for both states. The first is the state: `finished`, `started`, or `defined`, using the gate's started test for a live milestone. The second is a date: the finish commit's author date, or for a live milestone the author date of its `Milestone-definition:` commit. Then the title line, a blank line, and the finished bullets, or for a live milestone the `## Goal` section body read from the working tree, verbatim with its outer blank lines trimmed. Every print has the same typed header, an explicit state, and a date. A reader of the summary alone learns whether a live milestone already holds scope and how long ago it began, and it never needs to parse a field whose kind changes with the state. Each live summary costs two more path-scoped log reads (the started test and the definition commit). A milestone whose definition commit is missing, made by hand or cut by a shallow clone, needs a placeholder date. A finished print carries a `finished` word that the body contract does not need. How well this header lines up with the `milestones` line depends on the Milestones query line and Live line fields questions.

The first line is the word `live` for a live milestone and the finish date for a finished one. For a live milestone, the title and the `## Goal` body that follow are not read from the working tree. They come from the `requirements.md` that its `Milestone-definition:` commit added, read through `git show`, so both states are printed from history alone. The tool reads history in both states, with no read of the working tree. The live print does not change with uncommitted edits, and it comes from the same commit that dates the milestone's start. After any `Goal-revision:` commit the printed goal is out of date, so an in-flight reader such as the review pass's deeper read or a later starting-state read would weigh a goal the milestone no longer pursues. The print also has no source at all when the definition commit is missing.

The first line is the word `live` for a live milestone and the finish date for a finished one, followed by the title line. For a live milestone nothing else is printed: the query does not print the goal, and a reader that needs it reads `requirements.md` as prose. This rejects the draft's premise that a live summary prints the goal. The live print is bounded and small. It does not copy a file every reader can already read whole, which keeps to the draft's stance that the files are the record of live work and git the record of finished work. A `summary` call, and any `record` print composed from it, says nothing of what a live milestone is for. Every reader that wants that, the review pass's deeper read among them, needs a second read. How much of this reaches `record` depends on the Record composition question.

`summary` covers finished milestones only. Given a live milestone's path, it prints nothing on stdout and refuses with one `Error:` line on stderr and exit 1, saying the milestone is live. Live is told from finished only by that exit status. A reader wanting a live milestone's goal reads its `requirements.md`. This rejects the premise that the query has a live print at all. It is the smallest contract: the query has one print shape, the finish body with its date. There is no live shape to design, test, or keep in step with the `milestones` and `live` lines. It uses a refusal for a normal state, not an error. A chained `&&` read stops on it, and a runner cannot tell a live milestone from a mistyped path without classifying the `Error:` wording, which the fixed-line convention rules out. `record` and every caller that lists live milestones must skip them or handle the refusal themselves, depending on the Record composition question.

open-question.question: What is the composed shape of the `record PATH` query's print, how are one milestone's title and date, summary, and task lines set apart from the next milestone's, and is `record .` bounded, given that it prints every milestone from `milestones PATH` newest first and that this repository's record would hold 53 migrated milestones with their bullets and about 180 task lines?

Do the `gate` query and the history-side queries detect a shallow clone, whose truncated log reads every started milestone as unstarted so the gate holds no scope and drops finished milestones from `milestones`, `summary`, and `record` without sign, and if so how: refuse with an `Error:` line, warn on stderr beside the print, or state the limit in the help text only, as `tasks` does?
open-question.alternative: No query checks for a shallow clone. `gate`, `milestones`, `summary`, and `record` state the limit in their help text and the docs exactly as `tasks` does today: in a shallow clone the truncated log omits older commits without any sign, so the started test can read a started milestone as unstarted and finished milestones can be missing from the history-side prints. Detection is left to a later milestone, or to none if no field run meets the case, and `tasks` stays unchanged. Adds no code path, no git call, and no new output to any query, keeps every query's contract the same as the one `tasks` already has, and costs nothing in a full clone, which is every case this repository has met (its log is not shallow). A shallow clone (a CI checkout's default depth-1 fetch running a headless chain is the likely case) makes the gate pass a scope another milestone holds, so two milestones can work the same scope with no sign, and the record silently drops finished milestones; the draft's own finding is that the gate turns this from a short read into a sequencing failure.

Every query that reads the log (`gate`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`, and `tasks` brought along) first runs `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and, when it prints `true`, refuses with one `Error:` line on stderr and exit 1 naming the shallow clone and the remedy (`git fetch --unshallow`), printing nothing on stdout. The `tasks` help text's no-check limit is replaced by the refusal, and its five readers meet the refusal through the failed-read handling they already have (three stop lines, two prose notes). One rule for the whole tool and no silent wrong answer anywhere: the refusal is the existing failure shape every sibling tool and every chained call already handles, so no runner needs a new branch, and the remedy is one command. Refuses even a shallow clone deep enough to hold every relevant commit, and changes `tasks`, the second milestone's query, so finish, `derive-tasks`, and `submit-task` stop outright in any shallow checkout where today they run; one extra git call on every query.

`gate`, `milestones`, `summary`, and `record` run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` first and refuse with one `Error:` line on stderr and exit 1 naming the shallow clone and `git fetch --unshallow` when it prints `true`. `tasks` is left exactly as it is, its help text still stating the limit with no check.
